blocks.title: Diffraction
blocks.text: Diffraction of waves is the bending of waves around the sharp edges or corners of obstacles, or the spreading of waves beyond a barrier. It occurs when a wave encounters a physical barrier or an opening (a slit) that is comparable in size to the wavelength of the wave. The longer the wavelength, the greater the spreading, and vice versa.

Diffraction can be observed in various types of waves, including water waves, sound waves, light waves and electromagnetic waves. Some examples: hearing sound waves around corners or through a doorway from where they were generated, as sound waves bend around the corners; and the diffraction of X-rays by crystals, as the spacing between the regular arrays of atoms is of the order of the X-ray wavelength. Diffraction is a fundamental aspect of wave behaviour with many practical applications.

A ripple tank (Fig. 7.11) is a very useful apparatus not only to generate water waves but also to demonstrate wave properties such as reflection, diffraction and refraction. It contains water, a vibrator (for example a motorised oscillating needle), obstacles (for example a small rectangular block or a semicircular barrier) and gaps of different widths; a lamp above throws the wave pattern onto a white screen below the glass-bottomed tray. The vibrator creates a series of concentric circles or parallel waves, and an obstacle is placed to create a gap of a specific width; the experiment can be repeated with different gap widths. It is observed that when the gap width is small compared with the wavelength, diffraction is significant and the waves bend around the obstacle, creating a semicircular pattern; as the gap width increases relative to the wavelength, diffraction decreases and the waves pass through the gap with less bending. This demonstrates the qualitative effect of gap width on diffraction, and how the relationship between gap width and wavelength affects wave behaviour.

blocks.alt: (a) A ripple tank: a shallow tray of water with a vibrating wooden bar making straight waves, a lamp above and the shadow pattern on paper below. (b) Straight waves passing a gap about one wavelength wide spread out in semicircles. (c) Through a gap much wider than the wavelength they go straight on with only slight spreading at the edges.
blocks.caption: A ripple tank, and diffraction through a narrow and a wide gap (original diagram after Figure 7.11).

blocks.title: Example 7.6
blocks.text: In a ripple tank a wave generator produces 500 pulses in 10 s. Find the frequency of the pulses. Solution: n = 500 pulses, t = 10 s, f = ?. T = t/n = 10 s/500 = 1/50 s; f = 1/T = 1/(1/50 s) = 50 s^-1, so f = 50 pulses per second.

blocks.caption: Gap width and diffraction
rows: significant diffraction; waves bend round and spread in a semicircular pattern
little diffraction; waves pass through with less bending

blocks.text: Diffraction of white light by a fine diffraction grating spreads it into colours (For Your Information). The fine rulings, each 0.5 um wide, on a compact disc act as a diffraction grating: when a small source of white light illuminates a disc, the diffracted light forms coloured lanes that are a composite of the diffraction patterns from the rulings (Interesting Information).

blocks.prompt: What is meant by diffraction of waves, and for what purpose is the ripple tank used (short question 7.7; MCQ 7.11)? Why can we hear a person round a corner but not see them?
blocks.explanation: Diffraction is the bending of waves round obstacles and their spreading through openings comparable in size to the wavelength. The ripple tank generates water waves and shows reflection, refraction and diffraction; with gaps of different widths it shows that a narrow gap spreads the waves widely and a wide gap hardly at all. Sound wavelengths (centimetres to metres) are comparable to doorways and corners, so sound diffracts round them, while light wavelengths (about 0.5 um) are far smaller, so light hardly bends.

items: Diffraction: bending of waves round edges and spreading through openings comparable to the wavelength; longer wavelength, more spreading (sound round corners, X-rays by crystals, light by gratings and CDs).
Ripple tank (vibrator, water, obstacles, lamp, screen): small gap, strong diffraction; large gap, little. Example 7.6: 500 pulses in 10 s, f = 50 Hz.
